paras: The Jonesboro attack on the Thompson family was a night raid by about fifteen disguised white men on the cabin of Joe Thompson, a Black farm worker near Jonesboro, Clayton County, Georgia, around midnight on July 28, 1880. The raiders flogged Thompson and his wife, killed his daughter Millie Johnson and wounded his son Bob, reportedly in revenge for Thompson's prosecution of a white man. Militia guarded the arrested suspects, and Northern papers presented the killing as a revival of Ku-Klux terror in a presidential campaign.

According to an Atlanta correspondent, Thompson had worked a year earlier on James McElroy's farm in Fayette County, where McElroy's brother-in-law John Gray accused Bob of stealing a plow and beat both son and father. A letter to the Cincinnati Commercial instead named Gray as the employer. Thompson moved to Reuben Munday's farm beyond Jonesboro and had Gray prosecuted; Gray was convicted of assault and battery and fined $100.

Carrying kerosene torches, their faces streaked with soot or paint, the men broke down the door and tore a log from the cabin wall. Two of them held Thompson down in the yard while a third beat him with a stick, and others beat his wife until she fell senseless. Bob Thompson, about sixteen, was shot in the side when he tried to help his parents, and Millie Johnson, in bed between her two small children, was shot in the head and killed. Leaving, the band fired into the house of a Black neighbor, Clarke Goddard. The Atlanta Constitution summed up the night as "leaving one negro dead and three bleeding."

Thompson said he recognized Gray as the leader, and by the next noon the sheriff had arrested John Gray, Lewis Gray, Sam Cook and James McElroy. Reports of the number held rose to seven or ten, and Cook turned state's evidence before retracting and saying he had been frightened into confessing. A courthouse meeting of white and Black citizens, put at 300 or 500, condemned the crime, sought rewards and resolved to prosecute as if the victims had been white.

On the night of July 30 Sheriff Archer, fearing an attack on the jail, called for troops, and Governor Colquitt came with the Gate City Guard and took the prisoners to the Atlanta jail. Several Atlanta attorneys were engaged to prosecute, but no report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage through September.

The story ran by wire from the New-York Tribune on August 1 to small papers in Delaware, Minnesota and South Carolina, mostly as brief items under headings such as "Recent Tragedies" and "Murderous Barbarity." The Washington National Republican headed the Atlanta wire "The Threatened Georgia Lynchings," meaning the danger to the prisoners rather than the killing.

Northern papers treated the attack as political evidence: the Wheeling Intelligencer ran its correspondent's account as "KU KLUX AMUSEMENT," and a letter in the Chicago Tribune called it "the opening of the Presidential campaign in the South." The Inter Ocean, reprinted in Kenosha, said it showed "how the barbarism that inspired kukluxism survives," while crediting the governor. In reply the Vicksburg Herald told those "howling" in the North that the Jonesboro affair was no worse than a recent killing in Ohio.

Wire reports described excited Black residents surrounding the jail and demanding the white prisoners, and a Chillicothe paper called them "turbulent beyond measure." A Georgia letter in the Indianapolis Leader doubted that any jury would convict a white man for killing a Black man.

Atlanta and South Carolina accounts report one death and a son likely to die, while a Vicksburg editorial and a Chillicothe brief said two were killed. One digest dates the attack to the 29th, and the St. Landry Democrat traced it to Thompson's testimony in a justice's court rather than Gray's conviction. The Cincinnati Commercial letter said a large Fayette County crowd came to Jonesboro and demanded the prisoners' release and that local Black residents "raised no hand," whereas the Atlanta correspondent reported the Fayette band only as a rumor.

reader.title: Jonesboro attack on the Thompson family
bases: A disguised band of about fifteen white men raided a Black family's cabin at night, flogged the parents, and shot dead a daughter and wounded a son, in revenge for the father's prosecution of a white man (A7, A8, A9).

Millie Johnson was shot dead by a disguised band of ten to twenty men acting without any authority (A7, A8, A14); the papers give the motive as punishment of Joe Thompson for having a white man convicted of assault, and frame the raid as Ku-Klux-style night riding (A7, A9, A25).

An eyewitness Atlanta correspondent, the Atlanta Constitution as quoted, a separate Cincinnati Commercial letter and several wire briefs agree on the night raid, the beatings and Millie Johnson's death (A7, A8, A9, A12).

accounts.label: Atlanta correspondent (eyewitness to aftermath)
accounts.gist: Fifteen soot-streaked men with torches broke in, flogged the parents, shot the daughter dead and the son through the side, then fired into Goddard's house; the motive was revenge for Gray's conviction.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution
accounts.gist: Ten or fifteen disguised men left 'one negro dead and three bleeding'; seven white men were arrested.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Commercial letter
accounts.gist: A score of painted men flogged both father and son before shooting the son; Gray was Thompson's former employer; a crowd from Fayette County came to Jonesboro and demanded the prisoners' release.

accounts.label: Wire reports on the jail crowd
accounts.gist: Several hundred excited Black people gathered at Jonesboro and were feared, or said, to want to lynch the prisoners; troops were sent.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Intelligencer headed its report 'KU KLUX AMUSEMENT' and 'How Negroes are Killed for Sport.'
The Cincinnati Commercial letter in the Chicago Tribune called it 'the opening of the Presidential campaign in the South' and a return of Ku-Kluxism.
The Inter Ocean editorial reprinted in Kenosha called the raiders 'night-riders' and the attack proof that Ku-Klux barbarism survived, while crediting the governor.
Most papers ran short wire briefs ('Recent Tragedies', 'Murderous Barbarity') without comment.
The Vicksburg Herald, via the Louisiana Capitolian, called it a 'grievous wrong' but told Northern critics such outrages were as frequent in the North.
The Weekly Chillicothe Crisis called the prisoners 'cutthroats' but described the Black crowd as 'excited and turbulent beyond measure.'
A Georgia letter in the Indianapolis Leader called the deed 'diabolical' and predicted no jury would convict.

conflicts.note: The Atlanta Constitution and a dispatch dated July 29 place it the night before; the July 29 date appears in a later digest.

info: About midnight on Wednesday night, July 28, 1880 (an Atlanta dispatch of July 29 put it on 'the night previous'); one brief says the night of the 29th.
Joe Thompson's log cabin on Reuben Munday's farm, about two and a half miles beyond Jonesboro, some twenty miles from Atlanta.

Joe Thompson (about fifty, 'Job' in one brief) and his wife, beaten; his married daughter Millie Johnson, shot dead; his son Bob Thompson, about sixteen, shot in the side; the house of a neighbor, Clarke Goddard, fired into. Millie Johnson's two small children were in the bed beside her.

No accusation was made against the victims; the papers trace the attack to Joe Thompson's prosecution of John Gray, convicted of assault and battery and fined $100 for beating Bob (and Joe), after Gray accused Bob of stealing a plow.
White men disguised with soot or paint; Thompson said he recognized John Gray of Fayette County as leader, and one account says he also recognized James McElroy, Gray's brother-in-law.
One confirmed (Millie Johnson); Bob Thompson reported 'probably fatal' or 'fatally' wounded, and two later items say two were killed.
No report of an indictment or trial was found in the coverage through September 1880.
